details.title: La Marseillaise
details.lead: La Marseillaise is the national anthem of France. Claude-Joseph Rouget de Lisle, a captain of engineers, wrote the words and the tune in Strasbourg on the night of 25 April 1792, a few days after France declared war on Austria.
facts: E♭ major, as the French Army sings it
A march, about 120 beats a minute
Written in F major, C4 to D5

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: He called it Chant de guerre pour l’Armée du Rhin, the war song for the Army of the Rhine. It was printed without his name and dedicated to Marshal Luckner. That summer volunteers from Marseille sang it on their march into Paris, and the city named the song after them.

It was declared the national song on 14 July 1795. Napoleon and the kings who came after him set it aside, and the Republic took it back in 1879. In 1887 the War Ministry adopted one official version for military band, and a version for choir followed in 1912. The constitutions of 1946 and 1958 name it as the anthem of the Republic.

sections.heading: How it is played
paragraphs: At state ceremonies a military band plays it, very often the band of the Garde républicaine. The French Army’s own guide asks people not to sing while a military band is playing it.

The Army gives the key as E♭ major and the pace as a march, about 120 beats a minute, two beats every second. Of the seven verses the official version keeps the first, the sixth and the seventh, the one written for children, and a ceremony normally uses the first verse and the chorus. Valéry Giscard d’Estaing had it played more slowly while he was president. François Mitterrand brought back the quicker march, and it has stayed that way.

sections.heading: On the trumpet
paragraphs: Everything grows out of the figure on the first words, Allons enfants: a short note, a long one, a short one. Keep it crisp, a true dotted eighth and sixteenth, never rounded off into a triplet. The repeated notes want light, even tonguing so they don’t run together.

The chorus is where the work is. Hold the long notes on Aux armes for their full value, leave the rests in Marchons, marchons silent, then climb to the top of the tune on qu’un sang impur and come down cleanly to the last note. In E♭ the part sits low and comfortable, so the test is rhythm and a steady, full sound, not range. Breathe in the rests: after arrivé, after the first levé, and before Aux armes.

sections.heading: The instrument
paragraphs: Rouget de Lisle wrote a song for voice. The trumpets of 1792 had no valves and could play only the notes of their harmonic series, so a tune like this was out of their reach. The valved cornet, made in France in the late 1820s, changed that, and in a band today the cornets and trumpets carry the melody.

sections.heading: This part
paragraphs: The melody of the first verse and the chorus, once through, in E♭ as the French Army sings it. For B♭ trumpet it is written in F major, from C4 to D5.

sources.title: Élysée, La Marseillaise by Rouget de Lisle
Chemins de mémoire, La Marseillaise past and present

songs.title: Russia – State Anthem of the Russian Federation

details.title: State Anthem of the Russian Federation
details.lead: Russia’s anthem is sung to music by Alexander Alexandrov. The tune was first heard in 1939 as the Hymn of the Bolshevik Party and was the anthem of the Soviet Union from 1944.
facts: Written in D major, D4 to G5

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: Alexandrov founded and led the Red Army song and dance ensemble that still carries his name. Stalin chose his tune in a contest in 1943, and from the start of 1944 it replaced the Internationale as the anthem of the Soviet Union, with words by Sergey Mikhalkov and Gabriel El-Registan.

From 1990 to 2000 Russia used Glinka’s Patriotic Song, a tune without official words. In December 2000 Alexandrov’s music came back by law, and Mikhalkov, then in his eighties, wrote new words for it.

sections.heading: How it is played
paragraphs: The official score is in C major at 76 beats a minute, to be played solemnly and in a singing way. The government published arrangements for symphony orchestra and for wind band. It must be played at the president’s inauguration, at the opening of sessions of the Duma and the Federation Council, and at state ceremonies, and it is played at sporting events. At the Victory Day parade on Red Square a massed military band plays it without singers.

sections.heading: On the trumpet
paragraphs: The verse moves in quarter notes, with a dotted eighth and a sixteenth in the middle of most bars. Keep the sixteenth light and on time, leaning into the next beat. Recordings differ on where the dotted rhythm is used and where the two notes are played even; this part follows the official band score.

The chorus starts high, on written F♯, and later reaches the G at the top of the staff. The line is broad and legato and there are no rests until the end, so breathe on the longer notes: the dotted quarter at the end of the second line, and the half notes in the chorus. In the band score the other cornets and trumpets add fanfares with quick triplets during the chorus. This page has the melody only.

sections.heading: The instrument
paragraphs: Alexandrov wrote it as a hymn for voices and orchestra, the way his ensemble performed. In the official wind band score the B♭ cornets carry the tune, written in D, and the trumpets add the fanfares.

sections.heading: Rights
paragraphs: Russian law treats the anthem as a state symbol, so the music and the words are not under copyright there. IMSLP lists the 1944 score as public domain in Canada and the European Union, but probably still protected in the United States.

sections.heading: This part
paragraphs: The cornet melody of one verse and the chorus from the official wind band score, from the opening chord to the final cadence, written in D major for B♭ trumpet (concert C). The first ending, which leads back into the next verse, is left out.

sources.title: IMSLP, State Anthem of the Soviet Union (Aleksandrov)
Melody: cornet 1 of the official wind band score, typeset by kenta2/russian-anthem-kvzlyzug

songs.file: songs/The Star-Spangled Banner, American national anthem.musicxml
songs.title: United States – The Star-Spangled Banner

details.title: The Star-Spangled Banner
details.lead: The Star-Spangled Banner is the national anthem of the United States. The words are by Francis Scott Key. The tune is an English club song from the 1770s.
facts: John Stafford Smith and the Anacreontic Society, 1770s
Written in C major, C4 to G5

sections.heading: History
paragraphs: The tune was written for the Anacreontic Society, a gentlemen’s club in London that met for concerts, dinners and singing. Its song, To Anacreon in Heaven, had words by the club’s president, Ralph Tomlinson, and music most likely by John Stafford Smith, a court musician and member. By 1798 the tune was printed in American newspapers with new words of all kinds.

In September 1814, during the War of 1812, Key watched the British bombard Fort McHenry in Baltimore harbor from a ship where he was being held. In the morning the fort’s flag was still flying. He wrote his poem on 14 September, and it was printed with Smith’s tune soon after the battle. The song was in general use for more than a century. President Herbert Hoover signed the act that made it the national anthem on 3 March 1931.

sections.heading: How it is played
paragraphs: It opens most official ceremonies and sporting events, played by a military band or sung by one voice. It is in three, at a moderate, steady pace. B♭ major is the traditional key; bands also play it in A♭. Many performers hold the high note on “free” near the end.
When no band is present, or the anthem can’t be played, the armed forces sound the bugle call To the Colors in its place and give it the same honors.

sections.heading: On the trumpet
paragraphs: The tune spans an octave and a fifth, and that is why singers fear it. On the trumpet it lies well, written from middle C to the G on top of the staff. The opening falls through the chord and then leaps up an octave, so the low notes must speak at once and the leap has to land in tune.

Keep every dotted figure crisp: “O say,” “by the dawn’s,” “and the rocket’s.” The third line, the rocket’s red glare, climbs to the high F, written G, and the last line climbs back to it on “free.” There are no rests, so breathe by shortening the long note at the end of a line: after “light,” “gleaming,” “streaming,” “air” and “there.”

sections.heading: The instrument
paragraphs: Neither the tune nor the poem was written for trumpet. In 1814 army trumpets and bugles had no valves and played signals, not melodies like this one. The anthem came to brass players through the band, where the cornet and later the B♭ trumpet took the melody.

sections.heading: This part
paragraphs: The first verse, the one everyone knows, from the pickup to the last note, in B♭. For B♭ trumpet it is written in C major. The fermata on “free” is marked.

sources.title: National Park Service, Fort McHenry: To Anacreon in Heaven
Smithsonian, Why is the national anthem so hard to sing?
TAPS Bugler, The evolution of The Star-Spangled Banner

details.title: Long tones
details.lead: Slow notes to wake up the lips and warm the horn. Play each one softly with a steady, centered sound, and rest as long as the rest in the bar. Begin in the middle, go down, then up as far as the lips are ready for today.
facts: Middle: F4 down to B3, Low: B♭3 down to E3, Middle and low: F4 down to E3, Up: F4 to B♭5, Top: B♭5 to double high B♭6, Swells, soft to loud to soft: F4 down to E3

details.title: Lip slurs
details.lead: The valves stay down for the whole bar; only the lips and the air change the note. Every note in a bar is written with the valves of its series, even where the chart would finger it another way. Keep the air moving and the sound the same size from the bottom note to the top.
facts: Two notes, Three notes, Four notes, Five notes, Six notes, up to the 8th partial, Up to the top: the 16th partial, Lip trills

details.title: Chromatic ladders
details.lead: Every half step, one rung of the ladder at a time, from the bottom of the horn to double high B♭. The valves change on every note, so keep the fingers down firmly and the air steady between them.
facts: E3 to B3, G3 to D4, C4 to G4, F4 to C5, B♭4 to F5, E♭5 to B♭5, B♭5 to F6, E♭6 to B♭6, All of them, low to high, The whole horn: E3 to B♭6 and back

songs.file: songs/Warm-up/040 Valve crossings and finger trills.musicxml
songs.title: Valve crossings and finger trills

details.title: Valve crossings and finger trills
details.lead: Clean changes between fingerings: the valve goes all the way down and all the way up, on time, with the air going through the change.
facts: The hardest changes, Every half step, E3 to B♭5, Every half step, B♭5 to double high B♭6, Every whole step, E3 to B♭5

details.title: Octaves
details.lead: Each note, the octave above, and back. Slur them, then tongue them. Let the air do the jump and keep the mouthpiece still on the lips.
facts: Up: E3 and E4, to B♭5 and B♭6, Down: B♭5 and B♭6, to E3 and E4

details.title: Widening intervals
details.lead: From one note, out a half step above and below, then a whole step, and on to the octave. The middle note should sound the same every time you come back to it.
facts: Around F4, Around B♭4, Around F5, Around B♭5

details.title: Tonguing
details.lead: Short, even notes on a steady stream of air. The letters under the notes are the syllables: T is the tip of the tongue, K the back of it. Start slowly and keep T and K sounding the same.
facts: Single tongue on B♭4, Single tongue, up and down the B♭ scale, Double tongue on B♭4, Double tongue, up and down the B♭ scale, Triple tongue on B♭4, Triple tongue, up and down the B♭ scale

details.title: B♭ major, low B♭ to double high B♭
details.lead: The trumpet’s own scale, open low B♭ to double high B♭, every note: one octave at a time, then all three in one breath each way, then the whole horn from double high B♭ down to the bottom F, and last, slowly, a half note to every note. Rest a moment at the top of each run.
facts: Low octave: B♭3 to B♭4, Middle octave: B♭4 to B♭5, High octave: B♭5 to double high B♭6, Low B♭3 to double high B♭6, up and down, Every note on the horn: F3 to B♭6, Slow, a half note each: B♭3 to B♭6 and back

details.title: Major scales
details.lead: The major scale in every key. Each key goes up and down two octaves from its lowest tonic, then over the whole horn: up to the highest note of the scale at or below double high B♭, down to the lowest, and back to the tonic.
facts: All 12, from B♭ up by half steps

details.title: Harmonic minor scales
details.lead: Harmonic minor: natural minor with the 7th raised, so the scale leans hard into the tonic. The step and a half between the 6th and 7th is its sound. details.title: Hymns
details.lead: Four old hymn tunes, the soprano line, for a singing sound: long phrases, full breaths, no gaps between the notes.
facts: Melita (Dykes, 1861), Eventide (Monk, 1861), New Britain (1831), Ein’ feste Burg (Luther, about 1529)

details.title: Bugle calls
details.lead: The old calls of the U.S. Army, played on open valves: the notes of the bugle, B♭3, F4, B♭4, D5 and F5. Each call keeps the tempo of the manual.
facts: First Call, Reveille, Assembly, Mess Call, Attention, To the Colors, Retreat, Carry On, Adjutant’s Call, Officers’ Call, First Sergeant’s Call, Church Call, Tattoo, Taps, Echo Taps

details.title: Pedal tones
details.lead: The notes an octave below the bottom of the horn, played with the valves of the note above. Loose lips, a lot of slow air. They relax the lips after high playing.
facts: From each low note to its pedal, Pedal long tones: B♭2 down to E2

details.title: Cooling down
details.lead: As soft as you can, with a clear center to the sound. Lower and softer at the end. Then put the horn down.
